elements.text: Scaled Composites failed to consider and protect against the possibility that a single human error could result in a catastrophic hazard.
Copilot prematurely unlocked the feather system due to time pressure and unfamiliar vibration and loads.
Uncommanded feather extension occurred.
Aerodynamic overload caused the in-flight breakup of the vehicle.
Copilot incorrectly unlocked the feather immediately after the 0.8 Mach callout instead of waiting for 1.4 Mach.
External aerodynamic loads exceeded the feather actuators' capability to hold the assembly in the unfeathered position with locks disengaged.
Copilot experienced high workload from recalling tasks under time pressure and unfamiliar conditions, increasing error opportunity.
Scaled Composites' systems safety analysis failed to identify that a single human error could lead to unintended feather operation during the boost phase.
Scaled Composites failed to rigorously verify and validate the effectiveness of planned mitigation measures.
Scaled Composites missed opportunities to identify design/operational requirements to mitigate human error consequences during high workload phases.
Scaled Composites did not ensure pilots adequately understood the risks of unlocking the feather early.
FAA evaluations of the experimental permit application were deficient because they failed to recognize the hazard analysis did not meet regulatory requirements regarding human error.
Lack of direct communication between FAA and Scaled Composites technical staff interfered with thorough evaluation.
Pressure to approve experimental permit applications within a 120-day review period interfered with thorough evaluation.
Lack of a defined line between public safety and mission safety assurance interfered with thorough evaluation.
FAA did not ensure Scaled Composites was in compliance with mitigations cited in the waiver.
FAA did not determine whether mitigations would adequately address human errors with catastrophic consequences.
Pilots were properly certificated and qualified.
Fatigue and medical and pathological issues were not factors.
No evidence of structural, system, or rocket motor failures before breakup.
Impact point was consistent with regulatory requirements.
Human factors should be emphasized in design and training to reduce catastrophic events.
Experimental permit preapplication consultation should begin during the design phase.
Inspector assignment should be to operators rather than individual operations to improve inspection effectiveness.
A database of lessons learned would provide mutual benefits.
Emergency readiness could be improved by better use of helicopter assets.
Additional parachute training would have better prepared pilots for emergencies.
